speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: TABLING OF LETTER TO UN SECRETARY-GENERAL SUBMITTING RESERVATION TO ACCEPTANCE OF COMPULSORY JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are aware that the government has given notice of its intention to introduce today two bills dealing with protection of Canada's marine environment and the living resources of the sea. I wish now to table a copy of a letter which Canada's Ambassador to the United Nations has delivered to the Secretary General submitting a new reservation to Canada's acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice. This reservation is intended to guard against any possible litigation of certain features of these two bills.
Canada strongly supports the rule of law in international affairs. Canada has made known to other states that it is prepared to participate actively in multilateral efforts to develop agreed rules on the protection of the environment and the conservation of the living resources of the sea.
April 8. 1970

International Court of Justice
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)

Canada is not prepared however to engage in litigation with other states concerning vital issues where the law is either inadequate or non-existent and thus does not provide a firm basis for judicial decision. We have therefore submitted this new reservation to Canada's acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court relating to those areas of the law of the sea which are undeveloped or inadequate.

It is well known that there is little or no environmental law on the international plane and that the law now in existence favours the interests of the shipping states and the shipping owners engaged in the large scale carriage of oil and other potential pollutants. There is an urgent need for the development of international law establishing that coastal states are entitled, on the basis of fundamental principle of self-defence, to protect their marine environment and the living resources of the sea adjacent to their coasts.
In spite of this new reservation, Canada's acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the court remains much broader than that of most other members of the United Nations, and it is the hope of the government that it will prove possible to reach agreement with other states on the vital need to develop the law to protect the marine environment and its living resources so as to make it possible for Canada again to broaden its acceptance of the court's jurisdiction.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: TABLING OF LETTER TO UN SECRETARY-GENERAL SUBMITTING RESERVATION TO ACCEPTANCE OF COMPULSORY JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one would need to see the bills to which the Prime Minister referred and would also require very full information before making any kind of definitive comment upon the statement of the Prime Minister. We must recognize that it constitutes a serious step, a step hardly in the right direction, for Canada to reduce the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice. I am not passing judgment at the moment on whether or not this is the correct decision in the circumstances. I do say that the government has made this decision without any consultation with Parliament and without any discussion in Parliament.
It seems to me that the position the Prime Minister has announced today is diametrically opposite to the position he took in the House about a year ago when he indicated he was going to try to resolve all these problems 
through the United Nations and through consultation with the Secretary General. My point is that we seem to have here a complete reversal of position, without any real discussion in Parliament, on a matter that we all regard as very serious. The Prime Minister's statement does not seem to settle in any way the question of sovereignty. Presumably we are talking about control of the environment.
I want to know, Mr. Speaker, why the leader of the government has felt it necessary to take this position with regard to the United Nations and reduce the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice before the bills have been introduced and discussed. Why has he felt it necessary to take this action in an arbitrary manner without, if the government is going to proceed with the proposed legislation, giving an opportunity to the members of this House, the representatives of the people, to express their views on this matter before the adoption by Canada of a position with regard to the jurisdiction of the court?

speechtext: If there is any reason why this arbitrary action has been taken by the Prime Minister and the government before the matter has been discussed by Parliament, then certainly the Prime Minister has not given it to us. subsubtopic: TABLING OF LETTER TO UN SECRETARY-GENERAL SUBMITTING RESERVATION TO ACCEPTANCE OF COMPULSORY JURISDICTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TABLING OF LETTER TO UN SECRETARY-GENERAL SUBMITTING RESERVATION TO ACCEPTANCE OF COMPULSORY JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time in human history when every nation and all peoples in the world are seeking to establish an international rule of law, it is obviously extremely regrettable that the government of this country, a country which has a position of some importance in the international family, should find it necessary to reduce the extent to which Canada is ready to submit itself to the rule of international law.
I say to the Prime Minister that this matter should at least have been discussed at some length by the appropriate committee of Parliament. The reasons in favour of the need for such a reservation should have been given to us in full, with the officials of the government explaining in much greater detail than the statement now before us does the present legal situation, the present composition of the
April 8, 1970

International Court of Justice, the fears which the government has, and the validity of those fears. If every country in the world, every member of the United Nations, were to reduce the sphere in which it would be internationally bound every time it was faced by a matter of national interest, pretty soon the whole concept of the International Court and, indeed, of the United Nations itself, would be dead and buried. This is the issue which concerns us so very deeply.
I am not persuaded from the information contained in the Prime Minister's statement that the reservation is necessary. Possibly his advisers and he have studied the situation and reached a conclusion which may be valid. But I also say that as members of this Parliament I and all others who sit in this chamber have the right to possess as much information about this matter as the Prime Minister himself possesses in order that we may intelligently understand and evaluate the action taken by the government.
At least the Prime Minister should have had the humility not to do any double-talking in this statement. What nonsense it is to say, "Canada strongly supports the rule of law in international affairs", when in the next breath he says he does not intend to be bound by it. We should stop this hypocrisy in international affairs. There has been enough of it in the United Nations and elsewhere. I do not think we serve the cause of peace and international law and order by indulging in this kind of double-talking hypocrisy, and I resent it.

UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO HAVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seek unanimous consent- hopefully, the consent of the President of the Privy Council-to move a reference under Standing Order 43. My reasons are very simple and dramatically alarming. They concern the almost unprecedented unemployment situation in Canada. I am referring to the 6.5 per cent unemployment rate in Canada generally, the 9 per cent rate in Quebec, the 13 per cent rate in the Atlantic provinces, and the reported 22 per cent in Canada's newest province. This is definitely an unprecedented rate of unemployment.
My reason for seeking unanimous consent to move this motion is simply that the government's fiscal and monetary policies are continuing to have a tremendously detrimental effect on the Canadian economy. The programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion are not having any effect because they are not getting off the ground and offsetting the impact made by unemployment.
Since this problem is one that affects all Canadians, either because they are unemployed or because they face the danger of becoming unemployed, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski), the following motion:
That the chronic unemployment situation in Canada, which is especially serious in the disadvantaged areas of Canada, be referred to the Standing Committee on Manpower and Immigration.

I am informed by the Department of Transport and the National Research Council of Canada as follows: Yes. At a recent meeting of the International Civil Aviation Organization, of which Canada is a member, agreement was reached on a noise certification plan which will ensure that all new turbojet aircraft undergoing initial airworthiness certification after January 1, 1969 do not exceed predetermined levels of noise when taking-off or landing at an airport. With regard to the operation of supersonic civil aircraft over Canada: these aircraft will not be allowed to fly at supersonic speeds until it has been established that this will not be detrimental to the people of Canada.

The matter of genocide and hate literature referred to in Bill C-3 is of very deep concern to every conscientious Canadian. I speak with much feeling on this subject of personal freedom, individual and civil rights. As the result of my own convictions in this regard I spent 15 years, the best years of my life, dedicated to the premise that those less fortunate than myself were entitled to the same assurance of freedom and liberty that I have enjoyed.

One of the highlights of this experience was my opportunity to travel with a shipload of refugees from Nazi oppression in Europe who were picked up in Lisbon and Cadiz in January, 1944. These refugees were the first to reach the shores of their promised land, by the Mediterranean route, during the midst of war. I was part of that historic voyage.
At this time when the talk of civil rights and race riots in our neighbouring nation, the United States, is part of our daily headlines and the cry of discrimination is heard even in Canada, I think all decent Canadians deplore the dissemination of hatred. However, I am not sure that this situation can ever be better controlled by the implementation of this law. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), and I direct these remarks to the hon. minister at this time, have made it very clear in previous legislation which we have dealt with in this Parliament that the state has no business in the bedrooms of the nation. In other words, what they have tried to convey has been the fact that you cannot legislate morality; that you cannot, through the passage of laws, improve the nature of men or control their personal habits. In introducing this bill, they are inconsistent with that premise. If the state 
has no business in the bedrooms of the nation, it has no business in the living rooms of the nation or in the hearts of individuals. It seems to me there is a good deal of inconsistency as far as the government is concerned in pressing this legislation as they are doing. The roots of race prejudice go so deep that they are not likely to be affected by the laws that this Parliament can pass. I am convinced that only when people replace hatred and prejudice with love and tolerance will we ever eradicate prejudice, genocide and hate literature.
It is essential, and this is part of my own personal conviction, that human beings, divinely created with spiritual needs and potentialities, have inalienable rights which must be respected and preserved. I am sure we all agree on this. The question that looms before us is, how can this be assured? I feel sure that this was uppermost in the thoughts and minds of those who sponsored Bill C-3. I believe that those who have been involved in the long drawn-out deliberations over the past five or six years have been motivated by good intentions. However, good intentions alone are not an adequate safeguard.
The real difficulty with Bill C-3 is that it attempts to qualify freedom of speech. Freedom cannot be cut into pieces, discarding, according to someone's opinion, certain aspects and then retaining others. I was particularly impressed by some comments made by the eminent British historian Sir Arthur Bryant. In an article which appeared in the Illustrated London News, in 1964 he made the following statement:
But to render such incitement-
This means incitement such as Bill C-3 is attempting to eliminate.
-a criminal offence would be, so far as I can see, a denial of the very principle out of which the English belief and practice of toleration has grown. For the essence of that principle is that men should be free to speak and write what is in their minds without the interference or interdict of those in authority, and once that principle is denied, in the name of whatever virtue, freedom of speech and thought must very quickly cease to exist.
However deplorable such ill-education and prejudice, and however important it is to remove them by education and the active promotion of reason and humanity, to prohibit the public discussion of controversial topics because of their effect on vulgar minds can only lead to the establishment of the very despotism we deplore. The reason why the advocates of religious and racial persecution have failed in the past to win support for their vile, creeds here, as they so tragically have succeeded in doing in other lands, is because we have allowed freedom of discussion instead of suppressing it.

"Good beats bad where the fight is only free," we used to sing at my old school and it is true.
The true believer in toleration is the man who defends from persecution and victimization the very opponent whose opinions he most strenuously opposes. That is what in this country we mean by respect for freedom, and it will be an ill day for us if we ever lose it.
For every disseminator of hate literature and hatred in this country there are 999, perhaps even 99,999, who are opposed to and abhor such hatred. It is these people, so vastly in the majority, who will control the few who, because of the sickness of their own minds or hearts, are willing to allow themselves to become the disseminators of hatred and prejudice. I suggest to the House that the words of William Ewart Gladstone are very [DOT]applicable today. He said:
It is liberty-that fits men for liberty-liberty, that is, for every man to express his opinions freely, however unpopular, foolish or wrong-headed they may be. Everyone wants liberty to express his own opinions; the test of a love of freedom is a man's willingness to allow the same liberty to others to express opinions that he detests and despises.
It is impossible to have freedom of speech without having those who will use it for silly, irrelevant and evil causes. This may be a high price to pay, but it is the only true way to preserve the rights of individuals. No matter to what extent a man is wrong, he has the right to express himself. Any attempt to curtail the rights of a communist, Nazi or religious bigot is to also ultimately menace the rights of the sanest and fairest of persons. To attack the rights of one man, is to attack the rights of everyone.
Herein lies the chief evil of Bill C-3. There are others. In 267A(4) an "identifiable group" is defined as "any section of the public distinguished by colour, race, religion or ethnic origin." What is the definition of religion? Who is to define it? I might choose to define the communist ideology as a religion and then I might choose to condemn it as hateful and contemptible. The implications are ridiculous. How can this bill ever become a positive part of our statutes?

It was Lincoln who said that to sin by silence is to make cowards of men. In speaking to this bill, some of the government's supporters have referred indirectly to an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of Tuesday, April 7. They criticized certain parts of it but they never really told us what the editorial had said. Mr. Speaker, I am so convinced about the merit of this editorial that I intend to read it into the record in its entirety in order that hon. members may know the true gist of what the writer was seeking to convey.
"The problem of trying to render synonymous law and morality is that we then come down to the question: Whose morality? Whose standards of behaviour? Whose sense of morality? Who is to de*-termine the standard? Who is to attribute blame? Who is to say what is moral and immoral? Who is to decide when moral responsibility exists in terms of freedom of will, and when it has to be diluted in human terms because of environmental or physical causes?-In a pluralistic society there may be different standards, differing attitudes and the law cannot reflect them all. Public order, in this situation of a pluralistic society, cannot substitute for private conduct. We believe that morality is a matter for private conscience. Criminal law should, reflect the public order only."
This was the very argument used by the Minister of Justice when the amendments to the Criminal Code legalizing homesexuality and amending the laws on abortion and divorce were put through this House.
Did you support it?
I am thinking about horn members on the other side who then supported that premise and who now seem to be repudiating it by their arguments.
Did you support it then?

No. I stated very clearly my reasons for my not supporting it. Go back to the record in Hansard. There were other reasons involved. The editorial from which I have been reading continues:
The speaker: Justice Minister John Turner. The time: a year ago almost to the day. The occasion: the debate on the government's amendments to the Criminal Code liberalizing the law relating to homosexuality and abortion.
Now Mr. Turner is back in the House for the third reading of another amendment to the Criminal Code: the government's hate bill. However, he has conveniently forgotten the determined intention so often expressed by himself and Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau to separate law and morality. Mr. Trudeau's famous statement was that law doesn't belong in the bedrooms of the nation. But neither does it belong in the hearts of its citizens.
Yet that's where the hate bill would put it. The bill is a clear attempt to legislate morality. Its main section would make it a crime to communi-

April 8, 1970
Hate Propaganda
cate statements that promote hatred. Why? Not because anything follows from that. Not because public order is disturbed. Not because windows are broken or a mob becomes unruly. Not because anyone is endangered or because there is an assault or a trespass or a breach of the peace or even the likelihood of a breach of the peace. It simply says it is wrong and a crime to promote hate. Period.
In this context it has nothing to do with the public order.
That is the answer to the hon. member across the way who has been asking questions.
Our history is littered with examples of the futility of trying to regulate morality. As Harry Arthurs, Associate Dean of Osgoode Hall, has repeatedly said, it just won't work. Belief in this kind of law "rests upon a miscalculation about the efficacy of criminal law".
Mr. Turner recognized the truth of this and applied it in that same debate on homosexuality and abortion. He concluded by saying, "A penal law is not a good law unless it is an enforceable law. A law which is not enforceable is not a good law. The same applies here. And as if to compound the folly, the government would make the hate legislation even less of a law than it otherwise would be by saying that it could only be invoked with the specific consent of the Attorney-General. That changes it from law to political discretion. It would apply not to all citizens. It would apply only to the citizens Mr. Turner wanted it to apply to.
On top of that, even when he did apply it, the law would mean different things at different times. An escape clause says promoting hate would be all right-there would be such a thing as justifiable hatred-if it was for the public benefit.
Each judge, each jury, at each different point of time will have a different answer. What one day was an exercise in freedom of speech another day could become a criminal act.
Hatred can't be banned absolutely. At least the bill recognizes that. There are so many willing, even eager, to be roused to hatred over innocuous statements that an absolute ban would be terribly unjust. But in trying to define what is socially useful hatred the government has entered a catacomb of confusion. It ignores that social attitudes cannot be ruled by law and that the strength of a democracy rests on the sanity and reasonableness of an informed public.
Those words are profound, Mr. Speaker.
As a spokesman for the Canadian Civil Liberties Association said when the bill was before committee: "Many useful utterances in a democratic society incite what could be described, at the very least, as bitter feelings." It is the citizens, not the law, who must cope with these feelings. If they fail, then our society fails. And only the law will be left standing righteous and indignant and alone.
I might refer at this point to another editorial on this subject which appeared in the same paper on May 18, 1966. It reads, in part:
In Canada we have heretofore jailed people for offences they have committed. Are we now to jail

them for what they only intended to do, though the opposite may have occurred, or even to jail them for what they did not intend to do, and for what did not happen anyway? That is a net from which few poor fish, indeed, may escape.
What it comes down to is that truth and freedom are fashioned, always and forever, in a furnace of controversy.
This House has proved the truth of that statement over and over again.
Someone is always uttering something to incite somebody to hatred and contempt against some group or other, and sometimes it serves the public good and sometimes it does not. Therefore, if we create a law to stop the mouths of the ugly little neo-Nazis we create a law that sometime, somewhere may be used to stop other mouths-and those other mouths may belong to the prophets and the redeemers. In the past, they often have.
I would remind the Minister of Justice of the truth of that statement. I also wish to quote at this point the statement made by Dr. Frank R. Scott, a scholar on legal and political affairs. This is what he said when he appeared before a Senate committee in April of last year:
"I don't want the state in the sitting rooms of the nation any more than I want it in the bedrooms of the nation. I think my right to intellectual freedom is even greater than my right to sexual freedom."
This is the essence of his statement.
The protection of these basic rights must not include such action as would defeat its own purpose. With the greatest respect to the hon. members who sponsored this bill, and their reasons for doing so, I say that this measure, if enacted in its present form and if carried to its ultimate end, would result in freedom of the press and freedom of speech becoming a thing of the past. Extreme caution must be exercised; the outcome might be the suppression rather than the retention of truth and justice.
Again, I emphasize that within our free and democratic society there must not be a place for discrimination, prejudice or hatred, whether in relation to colour, creed or race. Basically we shall never achieve the desired goals of freedom unless men's hearts are changed, and the resulting attitudes permit people in all their diversity to live in tolerance and peace with their neighbours. The problem is much deeper than man-made laws can reach.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and my concluding statement will be short. If this bill were law, it could even put Dr. Davidson, the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation behind bars for many of the statements made on the CBC. For example, there was a CBC program last Monday night which attempted to generate hatred toward the citizenry of my own province, the province of Alberta. I doubt that the answer to racial hatred is a law which only emphasizes people's differences and opens the door to bigotry and endless litigation. All citizens of Canada stand equal before the law. It is my conviction that this is the best protection for every man and group within a free democratic concept.
I also want to tell the Minister of Justice that legislation such as this so-called hate literature bill would open the way for every imaginable evil known to mankind in our society, plus some not yet known. A virtual police state would be necessary to ensure that the law would be carried out to the letter. Censorship and book burning will only be a phase in the complete loss of freedom for every Canadian.
I do not speak as a lawyer, because I am not of that profession, nevertheless I am convinced that there are sections of the Criminal Code relating to the subject of criminal libel which do apply to the problem. I would appreciate it if the Minister of Justice would take note of this. Properly used, there is no reason to think they are inadequate to give protection to the person against whom hate literature is directed.
The applicable portion of the Criminal Code is found in section 248 (1) which provides:
A defamatory libel is matter published, without lawful justification or excuse, that is likely to injure the reputation of any person by exposing him
Hate Propaganda
to hatred, contempt or ridicule, or that is designed to insult the person of or concerning whom it is published.
Section 250 provides that:
Every one who publishes a defamatory libel that he knows is false is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years.
Section 251 provides:
Every one who publishes a defamatory libel is guilty of an idictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
Each time a new law is passed, for every right that is granted, a freedom is taken away from someone else. A law like this definitely restricts freedom of speech and of the press. The present law relating to libel maintains a most careful balance between private freedom from libel and the public interest in freedom of speech. New legislation will tend to upset this balance. The world does have evil people as well as good. The exposing of this evil is a matter of public interest, and even sometimes a matter of public duty, even though this may come within the technical category of hate literature.
We must recognize that deliberately false hate propaganda is sometimes used to bring discredit upon respectable and bona fide publications of particular political views. The technique used is to obtain a quantity of the bona fide material, and send it out with scurrilous hate literature to selected persons, who will then tend to associate the two. Here, therefore, the libel is against the victims of the hate, and against the bona fide publisher who is unfairly associated with this hate. Possibly there is need for greater protection within the law for this situation. This could be brought about by amending the present law, by extending it, rather than by replacing it.
In closing, may I emphasize again that within our free and democratic society there must be no place for discrimation, prejudice or hatred, whether it relates to colour, creed or race. Man made laws might assist, but alone they will never solve the problem. Christ put it clearly and simply when He said that "the fulfilling of the law is love. When hearts are filled with love there can be no hatred". Until they are, this problem will be with us. Moral problems are associated with the individual and are something which, in my opinion, are beyond the reaches of a law such as this. Therefore, in this respect this legislation is redundant.

Yes, I have more faith in the sermon on the mount than I have in any man made law. I believe this bill would defeat the very purpose for which it was drafted.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I welcome the opportunity to speak in support of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and to give my endorsement to the position which he has so capably enunciated.
To properly set the stage for my remarks, I should like to begin by concurring with members on both sides of the House who have stated categorically that they believe this bill is a totally unnecessary piece of legislation. I suppose we could argue the pros and cons of the intent of this bill until the next flood or until the cows come home-an expression we use out west-but I think we would still be left with the fundamental truth that no government can legislate the thoughts and emo ions of people.
At a time when members of this House agree that we are living in an era wherein we have many laws which are outdated, antiquated and ineffective, and at a time when we are in the process of revising and reforming the Criminal Code, the government sees fit to put another ill-conceived and unworkable law on the statute books. I feel that the government has simply become engrossed in the principle of ruling by divine right, irrespective of the consequences.
I am not a lawyer and I do not intend to concern myself with the legal ramifications of the bill. There is little doubt in my mind, however, that the best legal minds in this country will be hard pressed to make a fair and equitable interpretation of the provisions of this bill. Even here in Parliament where laws are made, it is difficult to find three members who can arrive at a consensus as to what the government is really trying to say in Bill C-3 or what it is trying to accomplish.
I am intrigued by the implication in this bill that any person who has passed the bar examination in any one of our ten provinces, and is admitted to practice, can then justifiably argue and adjudicate in matters of love and hate. For the first time in my life I am being asked to believe that human emotions can be directed and controlled by law in the same way as murder or auto theft, or other human acts. I reject this theory in totality.
Hate Propaganda
Many of my colleagues and other members of the House have taken issue with the so-called safeguards against the misuse or abuse of the provisions of this bill. Where the provisions of a law are open to individual interpretation and the application of such interpretations are left to the discretion of the courts and jurists, then there are no safeguards for the one person who is entitled to that safeguard or guarantee, namely the one who is charged under the law. We have here a law that seeks to control and regulate the emotions of love and hate, and a law that allows the courts of the land to interpret an alleged crime in any way it sees fit. I fear this bill is an open invitation to the commission of gross misrepresentation.
The bill states that a person can legally dispense inflammatory material about other persons and groups if he can prove that such statements are intended for the public benefit. It further states that it is not an offence if the inflammatory statements are factual. I wondei whether this is some kind of a new political or legal jargon. I wonder whether this is a new language that is being written into the statute books. I wonder whether this government is trying to perfect a new and unique language of law, all on its own. If this is the case, perhaps the government will also operate classes in this new law for the benefit of the country's lawyers and jurists. I find it difficult to conceive of any traditional lawyer or judge being able to discharge his respective responsibilities and functions equitably unless he is let in on the open secret of this new terminology.
I am puzzled by the government's position that it can legislate against such an emotion as hate without first taking steps to remove the motivation behind such an emotion. Hate is not a physical quality. Hate is an emotion, a mental quality. So this government is trying to control events after the fact rather than attack the root causes of the problems.
The bill is meant to eliminate or at least minimize the risk of riots or other physical violence by making it illegal to express such public criticisms against a person or persons or identifiable groups on the basis of colour, creed or religion or ethnic origin. Perhaps the one paragraph that should have been included was one to the effect that if the bill were passed we would have an instant flowery utopia.

Perhaps those who drafted this bill should have done a little more research into the effectiveness of other such laws already on the books, such as the laws concerning the illegal use of drugs, for example. We have strict laws with regard to the possession or trafficking of harmful drugs such as marijuana, LSD and so on. At the same time, the drug problem is becoming worse every day. But here again we find it is easier to have a law than to look into the root causes of the problem in an effort to find the motivation behind the usage of these drugs. Another example is the law which prevents farmers giving surplus wheat or other grains to their fellow human beings, even though these people may be on the verge of starvation. To me it is incomprehensible in this supposed age of reason, and in these times of alleged great affluence, these times when we merely pay lip service to humanity and humanism, that we should take up the important time of this House in dealing with a piece of futile legislation such as we have before us today. As much as I favour the efforts of mankind to eliminate hate and suspicion from the world, any attempt to legislate hatred out of sight and out of mind is an exercise in futility.
I dislike the word "hate". I would like to see it removed from the dictionary. I believe there certainly are other ways in which we can remove the hatred, if that is what we wish to call it, that exists in our nation and in other nations. Inequalities and iniquities of individuals in the same society are certainly the underlying causes of hatred and distrust. Any government would be remiss if it did not attack the problem from this direction rather than create a set of laws on top of the laws we already have. In this respect our present government is running true to form by taking the easy way out. As the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) capably pointed out in his speech last night, if this legislation is enacted the government then can sit back content that it has disposed of the problems of hatred and distrust among all our citizens and between our many ethnic groups.
I do not believe the problem can be disposed of so easily. Unfortunately, human nature cannot be packaged up and delivered in the right amounts to the right places when needed. Equality of individuals in their societies must precede legislation when one is dealing with human emotions. Equality means equal opportunity to act, to speak and to participate. Equality breeds respect for the 
April 8, 1970
individual. This is where the whole process of eliminating the root causes of hatred must begin. Before you have equality you must have mutual trust. That mutual trust can come about only through mutual consideration and understanding. Perhaps hon. members may feel I am somewhat old fashioned in my approach to the humanistic problems and perhaps more so because we are living in a very technocratic and complex age. Perhaps this is where we have gone off the track. I must confess I am old fashioned enough to still believe in the strong family unit as the cornerstone of any free and healthy society. We are all witness to the consequence of the collapse of the family unit as the basic unit in Canadian society. There is even stronger evidence of this to the south of us.
Do we need more evidence? Must we fall all the way to the bottom of the ladder before we realize we are losing our grip? I wonder how long it will take our present government to realize we must step back a pace or two in an effort to rescue the individual in our society from the oppressions of want and lack of equality of opportunity. I am one who believes we have everything in this country we need to eliminate the causes of hatred, the causes of discontent and the causes of distrust. I do not believe we need restrictive laws or legislation to control human emotions. Human emotions cannot be restricted. When one tries to restrict human emotions that are striving for expression in thought and ideals, I say one is inviting catastrophe. In Bill C-3 we have the seeds of an enormous catastrophe that will flourish unless we deal with root causes rather than trying to legislate against inevitable consequences. If the government is at loss for a starting point, if it is unable to establish guidelines for a program that would elevate the individual to his rightful status, I might recommend they start with the Ten Commandments. This set of basic tenets has served humanity well for almost 2,000 years.
Perhaps the government might re-emphasize these tenets and rededicate the citizens of this country to the application of the golden rule.
I do not know of anyone who has come up with a better set of standards for human conduct than these two I have enunciated. Of course, if the government should elect to try a basic humanistic approach to our social problems, this would be more difficult than pushing needless legislation through this House. But then perhaps it is time for the government to get up off its majority and get down to work. I could furnish the government

April 8. 1970

with a long list of names of my constituents who think the government should get to work and face this issue squarely.
To return to the provisions of the bill that would protect ethnic groups from insult, discrimination and slander, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) last night, I can only say that I as a member of an ethnic group am not unfamiliar with the consequences of human indifference or intolerance for others. I, too, have suffered some consequences of intolerance, bigotry and insult. My particular constituency is composed of pockets of people of various ethnic origins. But, Mr. Speaker, neither I nor my constituents have ever believed, nor do we believe now, that such influences could be legislated out of sight or out of mind. I would not be so naive as to suggest that I, as a citizen of Canada, would be a better Canadian if this law had been in effect when I was a young boy; nor do the people whom I represent feel they would be better Canadians if this legislation had been in effect for the last 100 years. Whatever insults they were subjected to have been eliminated only by hard work and by dedication to the basic human ideals in which they believe.
It is only by learning to appreciate the freedoms with which we are blessed that we can appreciate what it would be like if we did not have them. I say that chipping away at individual freedoms, such as freedom of expression and freedom of choice, will never restore human dignity or nurture human dignity. We need only restore that one quality that is needed to preserve our society and make it flourish. Many of my colleagues have mentioned the fact that we are being led by demagogues masquerading as parliamentarians. If this bill should become law and our fears concerning the real intent of Information Canada are realized, then there is little doubt that demagoguery will flourish in our midst.

I should like to speak in support of this amendment. I would say regarding the so-called hate literature bill that, however commendable its intent, I am convinced it is impossible to accomplish this intent by any legislative device. I believe further that the dangers of misuse of this proposed legislation far outweigh any small good that it might hope to achieve.
Hate Propaganda
The first thing that comes to mind with regard to a measure like this is a statement attributed to President Lyndon Johnson of the United States. He said that every piece of legislation should be examined, not in the light of the good it will do if it is properly administered but in the light of the damage it will do if it is improperly administered. I say that there is a great deal of legislation that goes through that should be considered in this light.
I can well understand the strong feelings of some members of minority groups, notably members of the Canadian Jewish community who back this measure. They have suffered much from organized hate campaigns, and even today I suppose they continue at times to suffer some embarrassment and harassment. I deplore this as much as any Canadian but I do not believe that a legislative measure such as the one we have before us will end this persecution, and it could well bring about for other minority groups the very oppression its supporters seek to end. To the best of my knowledge no similar legislation anywhere at any time has been effective in controlling hate. On the contrary, I can see the very likely possibility of this measure being abused to a great extent.
This bill defines an "identifiable group" as being one distinguished by colour, race, religion or ethnic origin. Where would this leave Negroes who, in some cases, have adopted as their slogan "kill whitey"? How would it help them? Would it not work to their disadvantage if they used this slogan? Perhaps even the more reasonable groups would find it would work to their disadvantage.
This bill makes it a criminal offence for anyone to incite or promote hatred or contempt of any identifiable group within the community, and inciting or promoting takes in everything, even to "gestures".
Back at the end of February-to be exact on February 26-there were newspaper stories in the Globe and Mail about a panel discussion at Halifax on the cultural and religious life of people in the Halifax-Dartmouth area. During the discussion a young black man threatened to bomb Halifax city hall if Negroes in the community were not treated more fairly. If this bill were passed he would be wide open to prosecution. Is this the sort of thing that Canadians really want to see happen in a free society? Who is to say where rhetorical emphasis, such as many similar threats of violence really are, ends and serious advocacy of hatred and contempt begins?

Over the past two or three years similar wild threats, similar appeals to direct action and the employment of organized intolerance and hatred have featured controversy in our cities, on our campuses, and sometimes in our politics. I believe that the existing provisions of our Criminal Code are quite adequate to control deliberate propagation of hate campaigns and the dissemination of the so-called hate literature. The more law we have on the subject, the greater the margin for abuse.
To my mind, education and the gradual achievement of greater mutual understanding remain the best and only true means of ending such social diseases as discrimination and inter-group hatred. The Globe and Mail issue of February 26 contained an editorial about Contrast, a newspaper for blacks published in Toronto. It referred to a cartoon in Contrast showing Abraham Lincoln in the garb of the Ku Klux Klan and suggesting that he had been "a white man's president" only. The same newspaper subsequently stated that "the resentment against and hatred of whitey. ..is becoming more widespread".
If this bill becomes law, will discussion of the tensions between black and white, which were apparent in the above quotation, be suppressed by law? If so, will such suppression merely build up pressures that will eventually break out in real and bloody violence? We wonder if this is the real aim of Bill C-3.
If we take a close look at Canadian society today we will find many examples of groups within it that are in a state of great tension in their relationships. Events in the Middle East, for example, have bred intolerable tensions between the Canadian Jewish and Arab communities. Are such innocent participants in this struggle as writers of letters to newspaper editors, who are often carried away into intemperate expression, to be prosecuted under this proposed amendment to the Criminal Code? What about the continuing tension between the English and French language groups? Are we going to prosecute the spokesmen of the native peoples who frequently accuse the white Canadian establishment of pursuing a policy of genocide? When we look at sbme of the statements of one of the Indian leaders, namely Mr. Cardinal, we realize that many of them can be termed inflammatory. How would they fit into the context of this bill?
We even have great tension and disagreement growing up between one region of Canada and another. No one can deny that

the West, for instance, is disenchanted to the point of talking about economic independence and even political and constitutional separation. Such a state of feeling breeds violent and intemperate words. Perhaps it is the intention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) to use this convenient amendment to jail western spokesmen who claim Ottawa is unjust and unfeeling.
There is so much afoot in our country today, so many areas of conflict, that hatred, contempt and ridicule are very easy to generate. But I do not believe for one moment that we can abate this sort of thing by piously passing an act of Parliament and then washing our hands of the situation until someone forces a prosecution against his adversary. To me, this bill is an open invitation to endless and barren legal disputes. All we are really doing is giving hatred and contention another dimension. Every group with a bone to pick with another group can now shift the battle to the legal and judicial arena. We would be far better employed in this House considering ways and means of broadening, understanding and modifying intemperate and dangerous public expression and action than in trying to legislate it under the rug.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
It has been increasingly evident, and not only in Canada, that we feel we can legislate almost anything away and that legislation is the salvation of everything. If we have this much faith in legislation surely someone, the government possibly, could place legislation before the House on prosperity. A bill on that subject would be about as impractical as the one we have here. During this session we have had legislation to improve the Post Office and legislation with regard to language. Has the legislation improved the mail service? Has it improved the relationship between the language groups? I do not think it has been any more effective in these areas than it will be-
They are great legislators. That is all they do.

-in the area of hate. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) mentioned a basic moral code and the ten commandments. I would add that what we need in this country is a basic pride of individualism, a basic pride in our country. This must be developed. We cannot continually downgrade our heritage, our institutions and the family unit and expect to substitute
April 8, 1970

legislation for them. We cannot make citizens merely social security numbers, entirely divorced from personal responsibility, and then expect to fill this gap with legislation.
When looking at the proposed tax reform I notice that the idea of treating the family as a taxation unit has been left out almost entirely. This is only one area that tends to bind society together. We may find that legislation in many other areas is not necessary if we can conduct our affairs in a manner to perpetuate the individual and the family unit.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from an editorial in the Globe and Mail of February 26, which I mentioned earlier. It reads as follows:
Democracy depends upon there being a public that is predominantly sane and reasonable. A public that can discuss volatile issues-that must discuss volatile issues-and find fair and reasonable solutions. If the government has lost hope that this kind of democracy can continue to exist then it' has lost faith in democracy itself. No law can produce this kind of public. No law can protect minorities where this kind of public no longer exists. There will always be those in whom hate can be readily generated. I assume that we should understand from the fact that no action can be taken, that the Attorney General of a province may grant or refuse his consent. How could an Attorney General refuse consent? After a complaint is lodged he has to investigate the situation. If we look at proposed Section 267BC3) we find that there are certain ways a man can justify anything he says. What does this all add up to? According to the hon. member who spoke before me this will mean that these people will not get the advantages, benefits and improvements he has suggested.

[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I suggest that you cannot legislate love and you cannot eliminate hate by legislation. This is something which must come as a result of the ordinary process of tolerance and association. I had a reasonable amount of experience in a province which has different races of people. There are certainly different ethnic groups. In the business with which I am associated we found nothing of any consequence in the way of differentiation between races and people. I do not think this exists to a very great extent, at least in my part of the world.
However, I am alarmed and concerned. I propose to support the amendment of my hon. friend from Calgary North and to vote against this bill. I shall do this because I am fearful of the effect it will have on freedom of speech, one of our most cherished liberties.
I have referred in this House before to a quotation from one of Shakespeare's plays, I believe Julius Caesar. One of the principals said, "How oft the sight of means to do ill deeds make deeds ill done". So, we have something here and it is said it is a great thing to have it because it will have a deterrent effect. I submit that it will not be a deterrent. The deterrence will be in respect of the person who wishes to express an opinion but is worried by a fear of the consequences.
In concluding these remarks may I say that this bill undoubtedly will pass. It is sponsored by the Minister of Justice. I wish he were not the sponsor, but he is so it will go through. I would hope he would recognize the principle that forbearance and tolerance cannot be legislated. So far as I am concerned, the difficulty and the danger in respect of this whole bill is that it may be a deterrent to individual freedom of speech and liberty.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on this particular bill because it brings into conflict two civil rights issues, the rights of minority groups as against the right of free speech. If we support the bill, then we say that recognition of the problems of minority groups has superiority over the right of free speech 'at this time. What makes the situation more difficult is, as has been so well pointed out by previous speakers, that this is a bad bill. The fact is that this provision of the Criminal Code in my opinion will be quite ineffective. I accept the theory that the bill will be useless in preventing the dissemination of hatred and if it is pursued vigorously
Hate Propaganda
will limit the right of free speech in this country. I think it would have been far better had this bill, in its present terms, not been introduced at all. The fact is, however, that the bill has been introduced and brought before Parliament and the people of Canada for their consideration.
Last night I listened very carefully to my colleague from Hamilton West to whom the attitude in respect of this bill is very simple. Does Parliament respond sympathetically to a bill, however weak, which recognizes that minority groups have problems? To him the vote on this bill will reflect our views on the question of the protection of minority groups. In other words, the question simply is, are we for or against the rights of minorities in Canada? This is the simple manner in which I feel I must vote on this bill. This bill having been brought before us I have no alternative but to support my friend from Hamilton West. My legal training, as must his, leaves me really concerned about the limitation of free speech, the possibility of witch hunts under the provisions and aegis of this bill and so on.
This bill, as are so many others which we are now considering, in typically Liberal fashion is vague, uncertain and hard to define or enforce. We have before us in this House several similar bills. I think of the Canada Water Act as one which is meaningless in respect of any effort to enforce it. I believe this bill to be in the same category. It is a grand expression of intent and a grand expression of an ideal without any way of ever enforcing it. No specific terms of enforcement are included in it. The provision which would leave to the Attorney General the responsibility of defining at what time or under what circumstances a charge could be laid leaves the enforcement of the bill wide open. No one will be in a position at one time or another to know whether he may or may not be subject to the provisions of this bill or whether he may or may not be prosecuted. I think this bill is a tragic example of the sloppy, vague and ineffective pieces of legislation we have had placed before us. On balance, however, I think, when we vote on the bill, whether it is a good bill or a bad one, we will be expressing whether or not we have sympathy for the problems of minority groups in Canada.
I must say I am convinced that the answer of this Parliament must be in the affirmative. If this were the only bad piece of legislation we have or have had before us I might be

April 8. 1970
Hate Propaganda
persuaded to vote against it. Unfortunately, time after time we are placed in the position of having to decide how we shall vote on bills which have a good expression of intent but which have nothing in them. I shall vote on this from the standpoint of an expression of intent and therefore I feel I cannot support the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak at this stage of our consideration of this bill, but I think I must indicate my thinking at the present time in order to show what I intend to do in respect of the amendment and the bill. I find, along with many of my colleagues-and this has also been expressed by some members on the other side-that this bill is a compendium of good intentions and sloppy thinking. The way it is drafted means that an attempt is being made to put on the statute books a measure that potentially could be a legal monster, a sort of Frankenstein. Why? Because it has been amply demonstrated beyond a shadow of a doubt that this bill, which on the face of it can be called just law, can be used for unjust purposes. As has been pointed out by my colleagues, most of the persecutions by government that have been known have utilized laws justly passed, but the people were persecuted thereunder in their application. This bill is of that genus.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Let us take, for example, a group such as the Hutterites in my province. They are a troubled people under constraint from society. However, they are a peaceful people. But I can imagine circumstances whereby, if the populace were not as enlightened or if the government should move under the powers given to it in existing legislation on the statute books of the province of Alberta, for instance, and if the Hutterites were to take overt action in protesting against the treatment they would be getting, an attorney general could then move under the terms of the act that is presently before the House to put them down further. Then, we would say: where are the rights of minorities? Legislation inscribed by the Parliament of Canada has been used to put down the minority.
Hear, hear.

This is not what we want. There is already in existence on the statute books legislation which achieves the main purpose of this bill. If our statute books were void of anything that 
would protect minorities, then I would say there may be a case for this legislation. There, I disagree with my colleague, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) because I do not feel a compulsion to have this legislation on the statute books. The bill before us is a sort of embellishment of laws we already have, but to me therein lies the danger. I would hate to think that those minorities which seek the protection they feel this legislation will give them should become the victims of that legislation in later years under some unscrupulous government or individual in that government.
It is for that reason-and it is a short reason-that I want to support the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). I fully understand the position of my good friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). I wish I could take him for a walk.
I wish I could take you for a walk.
Which of the two stays with the script?

That is a secret between the two of us. This position I can understand. But there are others who form a religious minority and there are those who are a political minority, yet why must any particular minority feel that it is aggrieved if this bill is not passed? I say that already we provide protection of minorities in this country. If we provided no such protection would our history be as it has been, and would it be different from those countries where minorities were persecuted? But minorities have not been persecuted here. The so-called documentation that was used as the foundation of some of the evidence-and some of it was pretty thin-for the Cohen report on this matter came from outside this country. I do not think that there was one iota of truth in the suggestion that the need for such legislation had its origin in this country. Why? Are we setting up an Aunt Sally? Are these to be straw men that we are legislating against? I do not think one should have to go through this process because someone suspects there might be a need for such legislation. I would say again that the inherent danger for minorities in this bill is far greater than the danger from which it purports to protect. This is all the more reason for supporting my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary North because legislation to

achieve the goal which all of us have, to protect minorities, already exists on our statute books.

That Bill C-3, an act to amend the Criminal Code, be amended by adding to section 267B thereof the following subsection:
If any person is charged with an offence against subsection (2) of this section, then the court may, if a breach of the subsection has been committed by the person charged or is reasonably to be anticipated, make an order in lieu of or in addition to the penalty set out in subsection (2) requiring such person to cease and desist from proceeding with or continuing or making any communication prohibited by the act and the order so made may be enforced as if it were made by the superior court of any province.
and that the following subsections of section 267B be renumbered accordingly.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on the last amendment we have had a very full and excellent debate with many high spots.
The amendment I propose is of a very different character to the one which has just been debated and dealt with. It is designed to strengthen the bill, to give greater remedies and more flexible penalties. Members who have followed this debate know that I have supported the principle and the spirit of the legislation and that in my view it is not such as to warrant the fears that have been
Hate Propaganda
expressed for it. The offences are defined in precise and clear language and it adds ample defences to appeal to those who may be fearful of its misapplication.
I support the bill, Mr. Speaker, but I do not feel any need to apologize for saying that it can be strengthened and improved by the amendment which I propose. This amendment deals with the appropriate remedy or penalty as applied to section 267B(2), the section which deals with the communication of statements which wilfully promote hatred. The proposal is that the penalty provided of liability to imprisonment for two years or punishment on summary conviction, in addition to which there may be a fine or a term of imprisonment, be replaced or enlarged by the right of the court dealing with the matter to make a cease and desist order; in other words, to enjoin the continuation of the offence.
Remedies are extremely important, Mr. Speaker. All sorts of legislation is rendered ineffective-and we are told this would be ineffective-because the penalty is either too severe or is inadequate. I suggest that if a person is found guilty of this offence it should be open to the courts to say, "We will not brand you as a criminal, will not send you to jail, not even fine you but will obtain from you an undertaking not to repeat the offence or, if you are unwilling to give that undertaking, we will make an order that you shall not repeat the offence." This is far more drastic and yet far more flexible and, in the end, a more effective way of dealing with this type of offence. It means that if a court comes to the conclusion that the offence was committed out of ignorance it could say, "go and sin no more". If it was committed by someone who did not realize the enormity or error of his action, he could be told to go away and not repeat the offence, without being branded as a criminal and subjected to criminal penalty.
I suggest this would remove some of the sting from the legislation for those who fear its application in too strict a sense. On the other hand, where there is deliberate propagation of material designed and calculated to arouse hatred there could be a warning that it must not be repeated. Then, if it were repeated the full power of prison for contempt should be used where there is a deliberate repetition of the offence.
In all legislatures, Mr. Speaker, it is a common practice to make laws and then forget about the extremely important matter of their enforcement. It is my submission that

April 8, 1970
Hate Propaganda
the additional remedies I suggest will make for a more flexible, less rigid, more fairmind-ed and reasonable enforcement of this legislation which I believe we are going to approve when the occasion arises.
I therefore commend this amendment to the House not because I think the legislation should be weakened but because I think it should be strengthened and I believe it would be strengthened if the courts had this power. At this stage of the debate I do not propose to go into this matter of law or argue the constitutionality of it. I do not propose to detain the House to argue on the legal implications of a cease and desist order or the proposals which I make. I merely say that this particular method of proceeding has been found suitable in provincial legislation regarding racial discrimination. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge the House to support the amendment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) for his ingenuity in trying to develop ways and means to deal with offenders under this act without actually invoking the punitive sanctions. There is some precedent for this under the Restrictive Trade Practices Act and in the anti-combines legislation there is provision for it.
I should like to point out, however, why I cannot support it. We could probably use existing provisions in the Criminal Code which, with very slight alterations, could be adapted to deal with the problem he has in mind. Reading again from his own amendment:
If any person is charged with an offence against subsection (2) of this section, then the court may, if a breach of the subsection has been committed by the person charged or is reasonably to be anticipated, make an order in lieu of or in addition to the penalty set out in subsection (2) requiring such person to cease and desist-
It is my proposition that we could make use of such sections of the Criminal Code as 717, 718 and 637, dealing with entering into a recognizance to keep the peace, which are simpler, far more expeditious and far more salutary in effect. If the conditions imposed in the recognizance were for a substantial amount it would have the benefit that those entering into recognizance for the person charged would have some pecuniary interest in insuring that there would be no repetition of the offence.
Now, I have only looked at these sections of the Criminal Code very briefly and we may well have to amend them. I do not believe in

having new and unnecessary laws-we have too many already, including this. I think, however, that we can make use of existing legislation to cover the situation where an offence has been committed and in order to deter repetition of that offence some order of a court is required. It may be that we would require a recognizance of this kind to be taken before a magistrate or a county court judge, but I would prefer that to what the hon. member has proposed in his amendment. This could result in a very difficult, complex and probably more expensive procedure and for that reason I propose to vote against the amendment. In addition, there are other proceedings to cover the situation.

Mr. Speaker, may I just say a few words about the amendment of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). May I refer to proposed new section 267c.(l). It reads:
A Judge who is satisfied by information upon
oath-*
That clearly means an affidavit, and is something we should take a look at. I continue:
-that there are reasonable grounds for believing that any publication, copies of which are kept for sale or distribution in premises within the jurisdiction of the court, is hate propaganda-
I am not so sure that the consent of thb Attorney-General is required in that regard. I do not think so. I continue:
-shall issue a warrant under his hand authorizing seizure of the copies.
Really, what will happen is this: Someone will swear out an affidavit that he has reasonable grounds for believing that whatever is in a package is hate literature, according to the formula of this bill we have been discussing for two or three days. I will not go again into arguments I raised before. This proposed section would give anyone the right to swear out an affidavit saying that he has reasonable grounds for believing that the material in the package should be seized. Of course it may turn out, as a result of a hearing, that the contents of the package do not come within the provisions of this bill. Would it not be strange if, during an election campaign, I were to swear an affidavit that the literature of the Minister of Justice, literature in a package, fell within the ambit of this Bill? Of course, anybody could swear out an affidavit
April 8, 1970

Hate Propaganda
that he has reasonable grounds for believing ment of the hon. member, to consider particuthat that kind of literature attempts to influence people.
Speaking seriously, though, this proposed section would confer tremendous powers. Almost anyone would have the right to swear to an affidavit, as a result of which material could be seized. I ask a very simple question. How are we to consider some of the books in our libraries? What about some of the books in the libraries of Canada? Is this the beginning of a new age? Is this the beginning of an age in which books will be taken out of our libraries because they may be read by speakers on a platform who would thus communicate, within the meaning of this bill, certain statements contained in those books to the people? As the hon. member for Peace River said yesterday, some of Shakespeare's plays may be affected. We need not mention their names. Somebody could swear out an affidavit saying that he has reasonable grounds for believing certain of those plays constitute hate literature.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Or, take Oliver Twist.

Yes. This provision could apply to Oliver Twist. The provisions of this bill will only enlarge the libraries of the court houses, or the number of books in the offices of court clerks. I suggest this shows how ridiculous this bill really is.
It is a straw man.

Someone said it is a straw man. But is it not ridiculous? And it is not serious when you try to curtail free speech and free thoughts which flow from books that may be in the libraries of Canada? To carry this thought a little farther, did not dictators burn books in order to curtail free speech and free thought? When free thought and free speech disappeared, you all know what disappeared with them: the people were put in the dungeons. They disappeared. I know that the members of minorities are worked up about this bill, but I say this bill will not work in favour of minorities. It did not take Hitler very long, after he became chancellor, to burn down the Reichstag and blame the fire on the communists or tear up statutes which stood in his way and incarcerate people who were protected by them in concentration camps.
I see no difference between a concentration camp in Siberia or in Germany. This proposed section is very dangerous, and I ask all hon. members, when voting on the amendlarly the wording of proposed new section 267c(2) which reads in part:
Within seven days of the issue of the warrant, the judge shall issue a summons to the occupier of the premises requiring him to appear before the court-
Within seven clays of the issue of the warrant you are to appear before the court. But, Mr. Speaker, in seven days a lot of harm can be done. That shows just how ridiculous this bill is. Not only is it ridiculous, but it is dangerous as well. We do not want a police state in Canada. Freedom will not result from it. I am glad I have taken the position I have expounded, and my conscience is easy. I respect the arguments that have been made on behalf of minority groups; I know how minority groups feel about these matters, but I am confident if they think this through they will see I am right.
Somebody in this debate used the expression "The dignity of the individual must rest on the freedom of speech." There is no dignity where there is no free speech and free thought. There is no free speech in the concentration camp, and there is no dignity. It just disappears where there is no free speech or free thought. Under this bill a man can swear out an affidavit of complaint, after which he has seven days to pick books out of Canada's libraries.
